_note: Milling of the staple grains into flour, which households eat, and bran, which animals eat. Each recipe takes one grain and the shaft work to grind and sift it; the grain itself is grown (wheat_kg, millet_kg, maize_kg). Maize is ground on a metate in practice; the shaft work and yield are the same order, so one recipe shape serves all three. Bran is a joint output with no reference price, a recorded waste (data/world/waste_heaps.json), fed to draught animals and herds (Complaints/544).

flour_kg.basis: per 1000 kg of sifted flour ground between stones from wheat, with the bran sifted out
flour_kg.yield_basis: MILLED AND SIFTED. Stones crack and grind the grain; the flour is bolted through a sieve and the husk and germ that stay on it are bran. Of 1190 kg of grain in, 1000 kg of flour (an extraction of about 84 percent; the wheat kernel itself is 80 to 85 percent mealy endosperm, 13 to 17 percent bran and 2 to 3 percent germ: Khalid, Hameed and Tahir, 'Wheat quality: a review ...', Frontiers in Nutrition 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9998918/, opened, so 84 percent flour is at the endosperm ceiling and a stone-milled bolted flour at that rate carries some bran; Round 3: The Fresh Loaf forum, a home miller, https://www.thefreshloaf.com/node/16879, opened: stone-milled grain sieved through a 55 mesh 'should have 84% to 88% extraction flour' after about 9 percent bran is sifted off first (a modern hobbyist analogue; 84 is the bottom of that range); roller-milled white flour for contrast is 70 percent in Hall, The Technics of Flour Milling, https://archive.org/download/technicsflourmi00hallgoog/technicsflourmi00hallgoog_djvu.txt, opened: 1000 lb of wheat gave '700 lbs. Flour', 188 lb pollard or thirds and 152 lb bran, so the 12.6 percent bran here is near that book's 15.2 percent; Evans, The Young Mill-wright and Miller's Guide, https://archive.org/download/youngmillwrightm01evan/youngmillwrightm01evan_djvu.txt, opened: a 5 foot pair of stones ground 'about 3,8 bushels in an hour', so at an ASSUMED 27 kg (60 lb) a wheat bushel about 100 kg of grain an hour a pair; the extraction is sourced within the modern-analogue label, the labour hours below are not, conf D), 150 kg of bran (about 12.6 percent, a little under the opened 13 to 17 percent bran share because some bran stays in the flour; conf D) and 40 kg lost as moisture and dust (about 3.4 percent, the few percent the whole-meal entry this replaces took as its loss; conf C, author's estimate). Shaft work: grinding grain between stones takes on the order of a tenth of a megajoule per kilogram of grain (author's estimate from the output of a hand quern at the 75 W a person sustains, about a kilogram an hour, and of water mills; Pass 11: Rachel Laudan, 'It's the shear bloody work of it: grinding', https://www.rachellaudan.com/2009/11/its-the-shear-bloody-work-of-it-sic-grinding.html, opened, a blogger's rough estimate of about 2 lb of flour an hour on a simple grindstone, about 0.9 kg an hour, conf C), scaled to the grain ground. The shaft work is priced through the energy market, so whoever supplies it (people at a quern or treadmill, or a water wheel and the millwrights who build and tend it) is paid there. Labour is feeding the hopper, dressing the stones, bolting and sacking, a few hours a tonne (conf D). Millstone wear is not charged. The bran carries no share of the cost (a recorded waste with no reference price); it is the winter supplement of herds and draught animals (95_herds.json, 94_agri_organics_gaps.json). Round 4 (Pass 14) labour: Evans, The Young Mill-wright and Miller's Guide (archive.org youngmillwrightm01evan, djvu text, opened), article on the elevator: 'Formerly, one hand was required for every 10 barrels of flour that the mill made daily; now, one for every 20 barrels is sufficient. A mill that made 40 barrels a day, required four men and a boy, two men are now sufficient.' A barrel of flour is 196 pounds, 89 kg (Wikipedia, Barrel, opened), so a hand handles 890 kg a day the old way and 1780 kg the new way; over an assumed 12-hour mill shift (labelled glue: Evans has a day and a night watch) that is 13.5 and 6.7 hours a tonne. The held 5.721 hours is within 20 percent of the elevator mill's figure and so is kept (a hand-fed mill without elevators would take 13.5). For millet and maize the same mill, extraction and loss figures are used as a stand-in (assumption: no separate figure found, tried: Hall on flour milling and Evans, both wheat; modern analogues for maize were not opened).

flour_kg_wholemeal.basis: per 1000 kg of whole-meal flour ground between stones, from wheat; the bran stays in, beside the sifted recipe that parts flour from bran
flour_kg_wholemeal.yield_basis: MILLED. Stones crack and grind the whole grain and nothing is sifted out: the few percent that leaves as moisture and dust is the difference between grain in and flour out (1040 in, 1000 out, conf C). Shaft work: grinding grain between stones takes on the order of a tenth of a megajoule per kilogram (author's estimate from the output of a hand quern at the 75 W a person sustains, about a kilogram an hour, and of water mills, a kilogram per few tens of kilojoules at the wheel; not checked against a primary source offline, conf C). The shaft work is priced through the energy market, so whoever supplies it (people at a quern or treadmill, or a water wheel and the millwrights who build and tend it) is paid there. Labour here is only feeding the hopper, dressing the stones and sacking, a few hours a tonne (conf D). Millstone wear is not charged.

flour_kg_millet_wholemeal.basis: per 1000 kg of whole-meal flour ground between stones, from millet; the bran stays in, beside the sifted recipe that parts flour from bran
flour_kg_millet_wholemeal.yield_basis: MILLED, as flour_kg from wheat: millet is a small hard grain, ground whole; the same mass loss and shaft work are taken (conf C, author's estimate; no separate figure found offline). Labour feeds the hopper and sacks the flour (conf D).

flour_kg_maize_wholemeal.basis: per 1000 kg of whole-meal flour ground between stones, from maize; the bran stays in, beside the sifted recipe that parts flour from bran
flour_kg_maize_wholemeal.yield_basis: MILLED, as flour_kg from wheat: dry maize is ground whole (on a metate in the Americas, a stone mill elsewhere); the same mass loss and shaft work are taken (conf C, author's estimate; no separate figure found offline). Labour feeds the stone and sacks the flour (conf D).
